# The Value of Disagreement: Why the Best Meetings Don't End in Consensus

## Rethinking What a Successful Meeting Looks Like

There is a common assumption, woven deep into workplace culture, that a good meeting is one where everyone leaves nodding. We celebrate alignment. We praise teams that "get on the same page." A meeting that ends in harmony feels productive; a meeting that ends in argument feels like a failure, or at least an unfinished one.

But this assumption deserves scrutiny. Agreement, it turns out, is not always a sign that a group has done its thinking. Sometimes it is a sign that the group has stopped thinking—too early, and often at exactly the wrong moment.

Consider what agreement actually tells you. When ten people leave a room all believing the same thing, one of several very different situations may be unfolding. Perhaps they have genuinely converged on a well-supported conclusion. But perhaps they are all mistaken in the same direction. Perhaps several of them harbor private doubts they didn't voice, because dissent felt socially expensive. Perhaps they agree on the surface while holding incompatible understandings underneath—everyone supports "the new pricing strategy," but each person pictures a different strategy.
